items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Should we embrace the layer lines instead of trying to hide them?
items.content_html:
DWdesigns:

It may take some time for the general public to embrace the layner lines as part of a maker-made vibe, but we creators can take them as what they are - a natural feature of the FDM printing.

I think we are comfortable at the point where makers can treat 3D printing as another tool in their arsenal rather than as a gimmick. We (well, many of you more than myself) know what our printers can excel at, and what the limitations still are. Prints that make the best use of the FDM method speak for themselves! So yes, I fully agree, a good print may have layer lines, but those lines are just a natural product of 3D printing, and not a flaw at all.

I can’t help but notice we are seeing more and more prints that have stopped trying to reproduce other building methods (injected, woodworking, sheet metal, whatever) and embrace the power and uniques that FDM provides. In doing so, the weaknesses of trying to use the printer as a hammer are going away. I really like how much people are putting artwork into the prints more now. I just saw @Josh-3D 's drum print. I can’t imagine who sees that in real life is going to decide that layer lines are detracting from how cool it is!

items.title: [blog.damonkohler.com] Running D&D Out of an Obsidian Vault
items.content_html: <p>A whole campaign — its maps, its monsters, its months of session history — fits in a folder of plain Markdown files. No database, no proprietary format, no subscription. The vault is the single source of truth, and everything else is a render, an export, or a link out to a platform.</p> <p>That constraint is the whole trick. Because every note is just text, the campaign gets a wikilink graph, structured database views, and an AI rendering pipeline almost for free — and it outlasts whatever note-taking app is fashionable next year.</p> <h2 id="the-vault-is-the-only-source-of-truth">The vault is the only source of truth<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#the-vault-is-the-only-source-of-truth" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>Everything lives in one Obsidian vault: campaign notes, NPC cards, monster stat blocks, loot, location descriptions, and a running session log. Every proper noun in the campaign is a wikilink — a bracketed reference that jumps straight to the note it names. Write “the party enters the mine” in a session log and it links to the location note, where the read-aloud text, the encounter, and the DM-only secrets are already waiting.</p> <p>That graph is the feature that pays off most at the table. A player asks about someone they met three sessions ago, you type the name, and the note is right there. No searching, no flipping through a notebook.</p> <h2 id="organized-by-place-not-by-date">Organized by place, not by date<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#organized-by-place-not-by-date" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>The vault is organized spatially, not chronologically. Each campaign is a self-contained folder, and inside it the notes follow a taxonomy borrowed from RPG video games — you travel to a place, you track an objective, you play through a scripted beat:</p> <ul> <li><strong>The campaign file</strong> is the novel: the planned story, its acts, and the plot threads still in play. It says what <em>could</em> happen.</li> <li><strong>Location notes</strong> are the zones. Each one describes a persistent place — the geography, the exits, who is present, the map — plus an index of what happens there.</li> <li><strong>Quest notes</strong> are the quest log. Each is an objective with a giver, a checklist of stages, a completion condition, and a reward. Some are critical-path, some are optional.</li> <li><strong>Scene notes</strong> are the cutscenes: the granular run-script for one beat. A trigger, the read-aloud text, a couple of skill checks, the branches, the tactical map, and a checkbox for each beat as it plays out.</li> <li><strong>The DM log</strong> is a scratchpad — one line per session recording where things left off.</li> <li><strong>Reference cards</strong> hold the NPCs, monsters, and loot for quick lookup during play.</li> </ul> <p>The key move is that run-scripts do not live inside the location note. A location is the <em>place</em>; the beats that unfold in it are separate scenes. Pulling the scripts out keeps each note short enough to parse at a glance mid-session, when you have no time to scroll.</p> <p>Those note types are wired together through wikilinks and metadata back-links into a spine: a quest stage names the locations and scenes it touches, a scene names the location it happens in, and a location indexes the scenes and quests that reach it. Any note is discoverable from its neighbors, so nothing goes missing under pressure.</p> <h2 id="database-views-do-the-bookkeeping">Database views do the bookkeeping<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#database-views-do-the-bookkeeping" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>Obsidian Bases turn note metadata into database views — tables and cards built by querying the frontmatter, the small block of key-value fields at the top of each note. A party base shows armor class, hit points, initiative, and passive perception in one glanceable table during combat. An XP tracker pulls from every character note and computes what each one needs for the next level. The numbers live in each character’s frontmatter; the base only queries and displays them, so there is nothing to keep in sync by hand.</p> <h2 id="the-art-is-ai-made-the-direction-is-yours">The art is AI-made; the direction is yours<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#the-art-is-ai-made-the-direction-is-yours" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>The battlemaps, monster tokens, NPC portraits, and atmospheric scenes are AI-made; the creative direction stays yours. A few small Python scripts call Google’s Gemini API, and each render is driven by a prompt written as a Markdown file kept in the vault alongside the content it illustrates — the prompt is where the direction lives, versioned like everything else. What used to take hours per map now takes minutes, so far more of the campaign gets art at all.</p> <p>Maps get one extra trick. You describe the layout in Markdown and include a DOT graph — a plain-text description of a graph, where nodes are areas and edges are the connections between them, with edge styles marking a path as normal, significant, or hidden. The model renders the art from the description; a second pass strips out any text and labels; then a precise grid, a scale bar, and column labels are overlaid to produce two copies. A DM version carries area labels and encounter markers. A clean player version is built for fog-of-war — a single image the virtual tabletop can mask and reveal as the party explores.</p> <p>The graph is what makes it work. Without it, the model produces beautiful art with nonsensical spatial relationships: rooms that should connect do not, or corridors loop in ways that break the game. The graph pins down the topology and lets the model handle only the aesthetics.</p> <p>Tokens, portraits, and scenes run a simpler path. A shared style instruction keeps a consistent dark-fantasy look across the whole campaign — monsters as full illustrations plus small circular tokens for the tabletop, NPCs as waist-up portraits plus tokens, and mood images for locations that want atmosphere rather than a battle grid.</p> <p>The result is not hand-drawn quality. It is consistent across the entire campaign and good enough for play, which is the trade that matters.</p> <h2 id="dd-beyond-holds-the-mechanics">D&D Beyond holds the mechanics<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#dd-beyond-holds-the-mechanics" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>Obsidian handles the flavor, the tactics, and the DM notes; the mechanical stat blocks live in D&D Beyond. Each monster and loot note carries a D&D Beyond URL in its frontmatter, so you jump from the narrative description straight to the rollable stat block. A browser-automation tool pushes vault homebrew up to the platform, rollable dice tags included — so “2d6 fire damage” becomes clickable dice on the character sheet. No copy-pasting stat blocks between two systems that both want to be right.</p> <h2 id="a-prep-pass-start-to-finish">A prep pass, start to finish<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#a-prep-pass-start-to-finish" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>A prep pass follows the notes rather than fighting them:</p> <ol> <li>Read the campaign file for active threads and guess what the party does next.</li> <li>Open the location and scene notes in play; write or revise the read-aloud text, place encounters, and set skill-check DCs.</li> <li>Generate any new combat encounters, balanced to the current party.</li> <li>Render the maps, tokens, portraits, and scene art the new content needs.</li> <li>Create or update the monster and NPC cards, then push their homebrew to D&D Beyond.</li> <li>Run a link-and-structure audit to catch broken wikilinks and missing notes before they surface at the table.</li> <li>Skim the party base for the numbers you will want on hand during play.</li> </ol> <p>During the session, you keep the scene note open and work down it, ticking checkboxes as each beat is revealed. Afterward, you add one line to the DM log and fold any improvised content back into the canonical notes, so the vault stays true the next time the party comes through.</p> <h2 id="its-just-files">It’s just files<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#its-just-files" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>The payoff is that none of it is locked up. Markdown, images, and a few scripts — it syncs across devices as ordinary files and it will outlast whatever note-taking app is trendy next year. The encounter generation, the homebrew publishing, and the vault cleanup are small AI-driven tools bolted onto that plain-text core, not the thing that holds it together.</p> <p>It’s files all the way down, and that is exactly why it works.</p>

The package {{Javadoc:SE|package=java.nio.channels|java/nio/channels|module=java.base}}, though sharing the name "channels", are not actually related; <code>java.nio.channels</code> are in fact buffer-oriented I/O classes.

=== Kotlin ===
The [[Kotlin (programming language)|Kotlin]] Channel API provides channels; while a <code>kotlinx.coroutines.Deferred</code> allows passing a single value between coroutines, a <code>kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel</code> provides a way to transfer a continuous stream of values safely. It is conceptually similar to <code>java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue</code>, but has suspending operations.
* <code>kotlinx.coroutines.channels.SendChannel</code> is used by the producer coroutine to push data using the suspending <code>send()</code> method.
* <code>kotlinx.coroutines.channels.ReceiveChannel</code> is used by the consumer coroutine to pull data using the suspending <code>receive()</code> method, or by iterating over the channel with a <syntaxhighlight lang="kotlin" inline>for</syntaxhighlight> loop.

<syntaxhighlight lang="kotlin">
import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce

fn main() = runBlocking {
val channel = produce(Dispatchers.Default, capacity = 10) {
for (i in 0 until 20) {
channel.send("Message $i")
}
}

// Consumer coroutine
launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
for (message in channel) {
println(message)
}
}
}
</syntaxhighlight>

items.title: [ifun.de] Amazon enables Alexa+ in the browser for German test users
items.content_html: On November 10, Amazon made Alexa.com available to participants in the German early-access testing phase of its AI assistant Alexa+. This means Alexa+ can now be used in Germany on a computer via a browser for the first time. In addition to the chat window, the website offers features for controlling compatible lights, thermostats, and security cameras; conversations, settings, and personal preferences are supposed to stay synchronized across the browser, Echo devices, and the Alexa app. Users can also upload documents, emails, and images, from which Alexa+ extracts information and, for example, creates calendar entries. At its launch in Germany, Amazon said it would store uploaded files and extracted content until users revoke permission. Access remains limited to customers who have already been admitted to the early-access program. Alexa+ is free during the testing phase and is later expected to be available to Prime members at no extra cost and to other customers for €22.99 per month.

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Sunlu FilaDC i10 dryer cabinet, and other dry filament topics
items.content_html:
In terms of a DIY automatically regenerating desiccator, you could cascade a few of these:


by 3D printing a tube that fits snuggly around them, and blow a low flow of air through them while they’re each hooked up to USB to dry them out. Only need to control low power low DC voltages, so well within the capability of an arduino with some mosfets or similar to manage.

I’d be curious how this thing is put together, but my guess is it’s just a PCB full of holes with heat traces that dance around the holes, much like the heated bed of old fashioned 3D printers, that heat up the desiccant beads during regeneration. Or maybe possibly a PTC heater inside, to further bulletproof against any possibility of overheating.

I only picked this particular one for illustrative purposes. There are plenty of others on aliexpress of the same or similar design.

KDE will decide by November 12 whether testing is sufficient to include it in Dolphin 26.12, scheduled for December; otherwise, the feature is slated for Dolphin 27.04 in April 2027. The view keeps parent folders visible as users move through subfolders and supports keyboard navigation, adjustable column widths and restoration of open columns. It is currently limited to Dolphin. KDE is asking testers to try everyday tasks, including using remote folders and dragging and dropping files, before the release decision.

items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A homelab enthusiast is retiring a Microsoft Exchange installation that began with Exchange 5.5 on Windows NT 4 in 1999. After migrating mailboxes to Microsoft 365, he kept Exchange 2019 running to relay local hardware and software alerts. Postfix on Ubuntu Server LTS will take over, with plans to add STARTTLS, Let's Encrypt certificates, and boot encryption

items.title: [smarthomeassistent.de] Smart Home News: Live Video for Robotic Lawn Mowers and Cameras with AI Features
items.content_html: Roborock is rolling out firmware updates in Europe for several robotic lawn mower series. They bring live images and remote control via a camera view in the app. A mini-map complements the video view; animations and text notices draw attention to approaching boundaries. A control panel integrated into Home Assistant also gets new features with version 1.4. Indian provider iDADA has unveiled new Wi-Fi cameras with AI features. The company cites local storage and a mechanical privacy shutter, among other features. The devices are intended to work without a mandatory cloud subscription.

items.title: [simon42.com] AVM rolls out FRITZ!OS 8.51 and no longer sends the DNS suffix “fritz.box” by default via DHCP
items.content_html: Since November 3, AVM has been rolling out FRITZ!OS 8.51 to additional FRITZ!Box models and the Repeater 6000. By default, the box no longer sends the DNS suffix “fritz.box” via DHCP. This can affect the accessibility of Home Assistant installations and other devices on the home network if they are accessed using a short hostname such as “homeassistant” rather than an IP address or a fully qualified address. Home Assistant OS 18.5 has also been released. The security update upgrades the Linux kernel on Raspberry Pi and Home Assistant Yellow to version 6.18.59 and fixes a vulnerability in IPv4 network processing. The fix was already included in version 18.4 for other boards. The developers particularly recommend the update for Raspberry Pis that are directly accessible from the internet or run on untrusted networks.
